title: Detection of File Transfer Protocol-Based C2 (FTP, FTPS, SMB, TFTP)
shortTitle: Detection of File Transfer Protocol-Based C2 (FTP, FTPS, ...
summary: This strategy covers the use of file transfer protocols for command and control, tracked as T1071.002, where an adversary uses FTP, FTPS, SMB or TFTP as the channel for instructions and data because these protocols are common in business networks and are rarely inspected in depth. It matters because the command traffic blends with legitimate file movement, and because several of these protocols support unauthenticated or anonymous use that needs no credentials at all. The telemetry that makes detection possible is network flow and application protocol metadata: firewall or netflow records with destination, port and byte counts, proxy or secure gateway logs for file transfer sessions, Domain Name System query logs for the server names used, and endpoint network connection events from Sysmon. The main way it fails is that file transfer is exactly what a great many business processes do, so the analyst must anchor on unusual pairings of internal host to external server, outside-hours activity, anonymous or failed logon attempts, and payload sizes that do not match normal file sharing.

beginner.definition: FTP, FTPS, SMB and TFTP are protocols that computers use to move files. An attacker can also use them to send orders to a compromised computer and to take files out. This detection looks for that kind of file transfer traffic going somewhere it should not. It watches the destination and the pattern of the transfer, not the file contents.
beginner.whyItMatters: These protocols are old and widely used, so blocking them is rarely an option. Many networks allow them inside and out for real business reasons. Some of them accept anonymous logins, which means no stolen password is needed. Traffic is often not inspected for content, so hidden commands pass through. Noticing the wrong pairing of computers is what lets you act.
howItWorks: Network devices record every connection, including the two addresses, the port and how many bytes moved each way.
The rule selects connections that use the ports and services linked to FTP, FTPS, SMB and TFTP.
It checks the two addresses against a list of approved server pairs, such as your backup server and your clients.
It looks at timing, because transfers at three in the morning from an office computer are unusual.
It also reads the protocol metadata, where an anonymous login or a large download stands out.
Where the destination, the timing and the size are all unexpected for that host, the system raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a factory with a delivery bay. Vans come and go all day and the gate staff know the regular routes. One night a van arrives and shows no paperwork. It takes a large load to a depot the factory has never used. The van itself is ordinary. The unapproved route at that hour is worth reporting.
takeaways: File transfer protocols are normal business tools, so the destination and the timing carry the signal.
Anonymous or repeated failed logins on these services deserve a look on their own.
Baseline which internal hosts talk to which external file servers before enabling the rule.

objectives: Name the file transfer protocols that are used for command and control and their usual ports.
Read network flow records and identify the fields that describe a file transfer session.
Build an allow list of approved internal to external file transfer pairings.
Recognise anonymous logon and repeated authentication failure patterns in protocol metadata.
Correlate a suspicious transfer with the endpoint process that started it.
Explain the risk of relying only on port based blocking.
dataSources: Firewall or netflow records with source address, destination address, destination port and bytes sent and received
Application protocol metadata for FTP and FTPS sessions including user name, command sequence and transfer size
Sysmon event 3 network connection with image, destination address and destination port on the endpoint
Domain Name System query logs for the server names contacted before the transfer session
Windows Security event 5140 and 5145 share access records when SMB is used to reach an external or unusual host
logic: The pattern is an internal host opening file transfer sessions to an external server that is not on the approved pairing list, particularly outside working hours, with a long lived connection, anonymous or repeatedly failing authentication, and payload sizes that are either very small and regular or very large in one direction. The fields to correlate are the source address, the destination address and port, the protocol command or user name, the byte counts in each direction, and the endpoint process behind the connection. Normal business transfers go to a small set of known servers, use named service accounts, happen in scheduled windows and move predictable volumes, while malicious use reaches new destinations, may be anonymous, and often shows a control style pattern of tiny regular exchanges or a single bulk upload. The distinguishing factor is the unapproved pairing combined with a session shape that does not match the business purpose of the protocol.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Unapproved external file transfer session from internal host
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: firewall
# detection:
#   selection:
#     DestinationPort: [20, 21, 69, 445]
#     BytesSent: > 5000000
#   filter_approved:
#     DestinationIp: ['10[.]10[.]0[.]20', '10[.]10[.]0[.]21']
#   filter_scanner:
#     Image|endswith: '\MsMpEng.exe'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved and not filter_scanner
# level: medium
falsePositives: Managed file transfer jobs that send nightly reports to a partner server outside the internal address range
Software distribution systems that pull patches from a vendor file server over an unapproved but legitimate path
Users copying large files to a personal cloud storage gateway mounted over a file sharing protocol
Legacy applications that use an external file server for data exchange and have never been documented
Network devices and printers that use the trivial file transfer protocol for firmware or configuration updates
tuningNotes: Build the approved pairing list from a ninety day review of actual traffic before enabling alerts, because legacy business transfers are the main source of noise and they are usually stable and easy to name. Scope the first rule to the internal host groups that should never talk to an external file server, such as user workstations and application servers, which reduces the population and makes the allow list short. Add filters for the approved transfer windows of each partner so scheduled jobs stay quiet. Require that the bytes moved in one direction exceed a baseline for that host before alerting, which removes small configuration fetches. Narrowing by host group means you lose coverage of server to server transfers inside your own network, which is a common lateral movement path, so keep a separate rule for internal file transfers between hosts that do not normally share files.
